paper.title_en: Probing the origin of the LHAASO Peanut with a hidden central accelerator
paper.abstract_en: A highly asymmetric, giant Peanut-shaped structure has been detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) in ultra-high-energy gamma rays at high Galactic latitude, $b\approx-17.5^{\circ}$, suggesting anisotropic particle transport around a Galactic accelerator. We investigate whether its spectrum and morphology can arise from a hidden central accelerator embedded in a projected anisotropic halo. The baseline model accounts for the diffuse strip and central excess, while a phenomenological prescription for a localized magnetic field reorientation toward the line of sight (LOS), together with a particle-conserved remapping of the electrons downstream of the far excess into an emitting column of prescribed transverse extent, enhances the emission at the far excess position. We explore various source ages, along with different combinations of ambient magnetic field strength and parallel diffusion coefficient, while accounting for radiative cooling when estimating the viewing geometry. The exploration reveals that relatively rapid parallel transport enhances the far component while preserving a dominant diffuse strip. Representative configurations remain compatible with the observed spectral energy distribution, although the fitted far component remains comparatively weaker than the central component above 100 TeV, even in cases where their component fluxes are comparable at 25-100 TeV. These results illustrate the plausibility of a hidden central accelerator as the origin of the LHAASO Peanut, while identifying the remaining difficulty in reproducing the relative brightness of its compact components within the adopted phenomenological framework.
